changes.from: ## From our own documentation
changes.to:
### The senses and the body (sensory integration)

Every child takes in the world through the senses and organizes what comes in so the body can answer it in a useful way (sensory integration). When that organizing goes smoothly, a child can pay attention, learn, plan a movement, be with friends and manage feelings. When the information comes in confused or distorted, the same child may struggle with all of those, and what we see on the floor is behavior.

There are more senses than the five we name with children. Sight (visual), touch (tactile), hearing (auditory), taste and smell are joined by two the body keeps quiet. Balance and movement, from the inner ear (vestibular), tells a child where their head is in space and how fast they are moving, and it is a foundation for the rest. Body sense, from receptors in the joints, muscles and tendons (proprioception), tells a child where each limb is, how much force to use and how to time a movement. A child who hugs too hard, crashes into friends, falls out of a chair or cannot tell they have been bumped is often still building that inner map of the body.

Pushing, pulling, carrying, lifting, digging and climbing send strong, steady messages through the joints and muscles (heavy work, or proprioceptive input). For many children this input calms and organizes the nervous system, raises attention and helps the body settle to a workable level of alertness. It works for the child who seeks movement and for the child who avoids it, which is why so many of our Idea bank cards lean on it. Heavy work, Obstacle courses, Swinging, spinning and hanging, and Calm body after big movement all carry it.

Children differ in how they take sensation in, and a few patterns help an educator read a child without labeling one.

- **Active and driving.** Learns through body and movement, always in motion, loud, intense, with strong feelings. This child craves physical input, has a high pain threshold, may not learn easily from experience and is quickly frustrated. What helps is a predictable routine, expectations in small steps, boundaries built into the environment, plenty of heavy work, swinging and climbing, a cozy enclosed place to slow down, and something to hold or sit on at meeting time (a wobble cushion, a weighted lap friend).
- **Highly sensitive.** Keenly aware of sensation, bright and creative, cautious, easily unsettled by noise, touch, surprises or a scrape. This child may feel things more strongly than the room expects. What helps is warning before changes, fewer and gentler sensations, a quiet corner, choices, and care routines done slowly and with the child's say.
- **Slow to warm.** Content alone, watchful, needs time, prefers one or two friends to a crowd, wary of surprises. This child may feel afraid or left out while they watch. What helps is time, a visual of what comes next, a rehearsal in words, inviting without pushing, and pretend play, art and music as doors in.
- **Under responsive.** Quiet, may seem tuned out, late to talk or to meet eyes, may not notice a hurt. This child needs more sensation to register it. What helps is bringing sensation to them, wake-up movement, strong tastes and textures, and heavy work before focus.

Most children show more than one of these in a week, and the patterns are a lens for wondering, never a diagnosis. Health and developmental questions belong to the family and their providers. What stays with us is the daily work of offering the body what it is asking for, and that is practice, so the Idea bank holds the set-ups.

changes.from: ## Partners in understanding
changes.to:
## Every body is different

Children take in the world through more senses than five. Balance and movement (the vestibular sense) and the body's own sense of where its limbs are and how much force to use (proprioception) shape how a child moves, settles and pays attention. Pushing, pulling, carrying, digging and climbing send strong steady messages through the muscles and joints (heavy work), and for many children that calms and organizes the body. Some children seek this input and crash, hug hard or never stop moving. Others take in more than they can manage and cover their ears, avoid messy hands or hide under the table. At school we read these as the body asking for something, and we offer it, a wagon to pull, a hill to climb, a quiet corner, a slow goodbye. At home a laundry basket to push, a backpack with a book in it, or a pillow fort does the same work. If you wonder about your child's senses, your child's doctor is the right place to ask, and we are glad to share what we see.

## Partners in understanding

changes.from: ### Assessing risk with children
changes.to:
### The six kinds of risky play

Ellen Sandseter, a Norwegian researcher, watched children at play and in 2007 named six kinds of risk children seek on their own. Each one lives here.

- **Great heights.** Trees, the climbing structure, spools and crates stacked by children, the top of the hill.
- **High speed.** Running down the slope, the tire swing, wagons and wheelbarrows at a run, sliding.
- **Dangerous tools.** Hammers, saws and drills at the woodworking bench, knives at the cooking table, shovels and rakes.
- **Dangerous elements.** The creek on walks, the pretend campfire, the hot dehydrator, deep water in the sensory table.
- **Rough and tumble.** Wrestling with agreements, chase, pillow crashes, the big body play of twos and threes.
- **Disappearing or getting lost.** Hiding places, the willow dome, the far corners of the farm, being out of sight and still heard.

Sandseter found that children feel scared and thrilled at the same time, a feeling they call scary-funny, and that they seek it on purpose, raising the challenge a little at a time until it feels just right.

### What the research tells us

Sandseter and Leif Kennair proposed in 2011 that this play has a purpose. Meeting fear in play, in small doses chosen by the child, may help children learn to manage fear and lower the chance of later anxieties (the anti-phobic effect). A child kept from heights may fear them longer, and a child allowed to climb a little higher each week learns what their body can do.

Mariana Brussoni and colleagues reviewed the evidence in 2015. Their review found that risky outdoor play supports children's physical activity and their social health. It found no clear evidence for other claims, so that is what we say and no more.

Angela Hanscom, a pediatric occupational therapist, connects risky play to the senses. Swinging, spinning, hanging upside down and balancing on uneven ground feed the sense of balance and movement (vestibular), and climbing, hauling and digging feed the body's sense of its own position and force (proprioception). Children who get less of this play are more often restless, clumsy and quick to fall, and the remedy she describes is more time outdoors, on uneven ground, with less adult direction. Beyond Discipline carries the senses in more depth.

Tim Gill asks the question that turns all of this into practice. What does the child gain, and what could go wrong (risk benefit thinking)? A hazard is a danger a child cannot see or judge, and we remove it. A productive challenge is a risk a child can see, weigh and choose, and we keep it. We aim for as safe as necessary, never as safe as possible.

### How risky play grows

Each of the six kinds begins at its lowest level and rises as children show readiness. Readiness belongs to the child, and it is watched rather than scheduled.

- **Twos and threes.** Low wide planks flat on the ground, short drops, slow swings, running in open space and stopping, sticks and small hammers with an adult beside each child, hiding where an adult still sees.
- **Threes and fours.** Planks raised on crates, the climbing structure to the top, faster swings and spinning, the first saw and drill with one adult and a small group, chase and wrestling with agreements, hiding places out of sight and in earshot.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Courses planned on paper and then built, high branches, knives at the cooking table, fire safety at the pretend campfire, creek walks with educators who hold water safety certificates, wider wandering on the farm with a plan for finding each other.

A child moves along this line at their own pace, and a child who climbs only to the second branch today is honored. The Idea bank card Risky play set-ups holds the set-ups and the agreements for each kind.

changes.from: The input tends to help a child feel organized for a while after the work, so we offer it before transitions and quiet times.
changes.to: The input tends to help a child feel organized for a while after the work, so we offer it before transitions and quiet times. Occupational therapists offer a few guidelines we follow. Set times in the day for heavy work and let children know they are coming. The child chooses the work from a few options and leads it, and when a child says more we continue, and when they say stop or show it, we stop at once. Watch the face. A happy or relaxed face means the work is right, and whimpers, a blank look or wild laughter mean the body has had enough. A worn or carried weight, such as a backpack with a book or a water bottle, stays under about one twentieth of the child's own weight, so a forty pound child carries two pounds, and a vest or snug clothing can give the same pressure without weight. Less is more, and the simplest set-up is usually the best one.

changes.from: Calm tools are offered and never required, and a child is never sent away to calm alone.
changes.to: Calm tools are offered and never required, and a child is never sent away to calm alone. A weighted lap friend can be made at school from a sock or a pillowcase filled with rice or beans and tied or sewn shut, kept to a pound or two, and offered for a child's lap at meeting time or rest, never on the head or chest. A chair with sides, a cube chair or a wobble cushion gives a child who wiggles something to push against while they stay with the group.

changes.from: Keep heavy blankets off the head and face, let your child push them off alone, and never use them for sleep.
changes.to: Keep heavy blankets off the head and face, let your child push them off alone, and never use them for sleep. A weighted lap friend made from a sock filled with rice and tied shut, resting on your child's lap at the table or in the car, gives the same steady pressure, and a backpack with one book in it is heavy work on the walk in.

changes.from: Agree with children on how to use it and how many fit inside at once.
changes.to: Agree with children on how to use it and how many fit inside at once. A small tent or a corner closed on three sides lowers what the eyes take in, which helps a child who is taking in more than they can manage. A chair with sides, a cube chair or a beanbag gives a child who wiggles something to push against, and a weighted lap friend made from a sock of rice can rest on a lap there.

changes.from: The child may be looking for strong body pressure (proprioception). They may have trouble judging how close others are (visual-spatial). Crashing might also be a way to connect and play.
changes.to: The child may be looking for strong body pressure (proprioception). They may have trouble judging how close others are (visual-spatial). Crashing might also be a way to connect and play. This is often the active and driving pattern, a body that craves strong input, and heavy work set up at the start of the day meets it before it spills onto friends.

changes.from: Children may be exploring power, strength and closeness. Rough play gives strong body input (proprioception) and practice reading others' signals. When it goes too far, a child might not yet notice when their body or their friend's body has had enough (interoception).
changes.to: Children may be exploring power, strength and closeness. Rough play gives strong body input (proprioception) and practice reading others' signals. When it goes too far, a child might not yet notice when their body or their friend's body has had enough (interoception). In the active and driving pattern the child has a high threshold for sensation and may not feel a friend's limit, so agreements for wrestling and a crash spot give the input a place.

changes.from: The child may be seeking height and the thrill of being up high (vestibular). Climbing may give the whole body strong work (proprioception). The child might also want to see the room from a new view.

The child might also want to see the room from a new view. In the active and driving pattern the body is asking for height and climbing, and a place where climbing is allowed answers it.

This is often the highly sensitive pattern, a child who takes in more sound than the room expects, and a quiet corner or warning before loud moments helps.

changes.from: The child may be seeking a calm, enclosed space when the room feels too busy (avoiding sensation). Small spaces may give the body a feeling of safety and pressure (proprioception). The child might also be playing a game of hiding and being found.
changes.to: The child may be seeking a calm, enclosed space when the room feels too busy (avoiding sensation). Small spaces may give the body a feeling of safety and pressure (proprioception). A highly sensitive child may be lowering what the eyes and ears take in, and a tent or a cozy corner closed on three sides offers the same with company nearby.

changes.from: The child may find wet, sticky or gritty feelings too strong (tactile). Messy materials may feel unpredictable. The child might also be watching first to learn how it works.
changes.to: The child may find wet, sticky or gritty feelings too strong (tactile). Messy materials may feel unpredictable. The child might also be watching first to learn how it works. This is often the highly sensitive pattern, where touch feels stronger than it does to others, and a tool, a glove or a dry version of the material lets the child take part on their own terms.

changes.from: The child may find tags, seams or textures too scratchy or tight (tactile). Bare feet may help them feel the ground (proprioception). They might also be warm or seeking freedom.
changes.to: The child may find tags, seams or textures too scratchy or tight (tactile). Bare feet may help them feel the ground (proprioception). They might also be warm or seeking freedom. A highly sensitive child may feel seams and tags as more than they can bear, and soft clothes without tags or socks turned inside out are small fixes families can try.

changes.from: The child may need to feel safe before exploring. They may be missing family. They might also find the room or group too much (avoiding sensation).
changes.to: The child may need to feel safe before exploring. They may be missing family. They might also find the room or group too much (avoiding sensation). This may be the slow to warm pattern, a child who needs time and a rehearsal in words of what comes next before joining, and who does best invited and never pushed.

changes.from: The child may find groups too loud or busy (avoiding sensation). They may be watching and learning before joining. They might also prefer quiet play.
changes.to: The child may find groups too loud or busy (avoiding sensation). They may be watching and learning before joining. They might also prefer quiet play. This may be the slow to warm pattern, where watching first is the child's way in, and pretend play, art and music are quieter doors into the group.

changes.from: The child may be unsure what to do or how to join. The room might feel too busy (avoiding sensation). They might also be watching and learning before they join.
changes.to: The child may be unsure what to do or how to join. The room might feel too busy (avoiding sensation). They might also be watching and learning before they join. This may be the under responsive pattern, a child who needs more sensation to register it, and bringing strong textures, movement and heavy work to the child can wake the body for play.

changes.from: The body may be seeking pressure from the floor to feel calm (proprioception). The child may be tired or low on energy (interoception). It might also be a way to say no or to rest when things feel like too much.
changes.to: The body may be seeking pressure from the floor to feel calm (proprioception). The child may be tired or low on energy (interoception). It might also be a way to say no or to rest when things feel like too much. In the under responsive pattern the body registers less and needs more input to feel alert, and heavy work, strong tastes or wake-up movement before a focused time helps.

changes.from: The body may be seeking pressure to feel calm or steady (proprioception). The child may be tired or low on energy (interoception). Leaning might also be a way to connect and feel close.
changes.to: The body may be seeking pressure to feel calm or steady (proprioception). The child may be tired or low on energy (interoception). Leaning might also be a way to connect and feel close. In the under responsive pattern the child may be looking for pressure the body is not getting on its own, and a weighted lap friend, a wall to push or a chair with sides gives it.

changes.from: The child may find changes hard to predict and feel unsafe. Sameness may help them feel calm (self-regulation). They might also have been holding many feelings already.
changes.to: The child may find changes hard to predict and feel unsafe. Sameness may help them feel calm (self-regulation). They might also have been holding many feelings already. This is often the highly sensitive pattern, where surprises land hard, and a warning before a change and a picture of what comes next make the change smaller.

changes.from: The body may be seeking movement to stay alert (vestibular). Tipping may help the child focus (self-regulation). The child might also be testing balance and risk.
changes.to: The body may be seeking movement to stay alert (vestibular). Tipping may help the child focus (self-regulation). The child might also be testing balance and risk. A body asking for movement while it sits, which a wobble cushion or a chair with sides can answer without leaving the group.

changes.from: The body may be seeking movement that helps it feel calm or alert (vestibular). Rocking may be soothing when things feel like too much (self-regulation). The child might also enjoy the dizzy feeling.
changes.to: The body may be seeking movement that helps it feel calm or alert (vestibular). Rocking may be soothing when things feel like too much (self-regulation). The child might also enjoy the dizzy feeling. Spinning feeds the sense of balance and movement (vestibular), and a swing or a place to spin safely gives it on purpose before meeting time.
